b: Irrigation: artificial application of water to soil to meet crop water needs.
Need: inadequate/uneven rainfall, commercial crops, multiple cropping, controlled water supply.
Benefits: higher yield, famine protection, hydropower, navigation, domestic water, revenue.
Ill effects: waterlogging, salinity/alkalinity, mosquito breeding, cold & damp climate.
Flow irrigation: water flows by gravity. (a) Perennial – continuous supply from weir/barrage/storage; (b) Inundation/flood – canals run only in high river stages, no headworks.
Lift irrigation: water lifted by pumps/wells/tube wells.
Storage irrigation: dam built to store water, released as needed.
Direct irrigation: water diverted directly from river by weir/barrage (no storage).
Surface: free/wild flooding (cheapest, least efficient), border strip, check basin, basin (orchards), furrow (row crops: maize, cotton, potato).
Subsurface: water applied below ground; water table raised to root zone.
Sprinkler: water sprayed like rain; for undulating land, sandy soils; efficiency ≈ 70–80%.
Drip / trickle: water at root zone drop by drop; highest efficiency ≈ 90%+; suits saline water, orchards, vegetables, arid areas.
Kharif (summer): Apr–Sep — rice, cotton, maize, sugarcane (sown), millets.
Rabi (winter): Oct–Mar — wheat, gram, barley, mustard, oilseeds.
Perennial crops: sugarcane, orchards (need water whole year).
Cash crops: cotton, sugarcane, tobacco. Fodder: berseem, jowar.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Sprinkler system: Pump + main + laterals + risers + nozzles; application efficiency ≈ 70–80%; suits sandy/undulating land, closely spaced crops; not good in high wind.
Drip system: Mains, sub-mains, laterals, emitters (≈ 2–8 L/h); efficiency ≈ 90%; needs filters (screen/sand/disc) against clogging; ideal for orchards, vegetables, saline water.
Furrow / border / basin: Furrows for row crops (cotton, maize); borders (strips) for wheat, fodder; check basins for orchards.
Inundation canals: Take off from river without weir; flow only when river is high (flood season); Sindh had many before barrages.
Water-use priority: Pakistan agriculture uses ≈ 90%+ of withdrawals — hence efficiency improvement (lining, laser levelling, drip) matters most.
Efficiency order: drip > sprinkler > furrow/border > flooding. Lift irrigation = tube wells/pumps; storage irrigation = dams.
Saturation capacity: all pores filled with water.
Gravity water: drains freely after saturation; not useful to plants.
Field capacity (FC): water held after gravity drainage stops (≈ 1–3 days after irrigation).
Permanent wilting point (PWP): moisture below which plants cannot extract water and wilt permanently.
Available moisture = FC − PWP (also called capillary water available to plants).
Readily available moisture (RAM): ≈ 75–80% of available moisture; irrigation applied before this is used up.
Hygroscopic water: thin film held tightly on particles; not available to plants.
Optimum moisture content: moisture at which crop gives maximum yield.
Depth of water held in root zone
f = d_w / Cu (Cu = daily consumptive use)
Consumptive use (Cu): water used by plant (transpiration) + evaporation from soil + water in plant tissue.
Effective rainfall: part of rainfall useful for crop needs.
Net irrigation requirement (NIR) = CIR + leaching requirement + other needs.
Methods: Blaney–Criddle (Cu = k·f; f = Σ p(1.8t+32)/100, inches), Penman (energy balance, most accurate), Hargreaves, Thornthwaite, lysimeter (direct measurement).

Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Depth of water stored in root zone: d = (γd/γw) · D · (FC − m) — where D = root-zone depth, m = moisture content before irrigation.
Frequency of irrigation: Interval (days) = depth of readily available water ÷ daily consumptive use.
Penman / modified Penman: Most accurate ETo method (radiation + wind + humidity + temperature); Hargreaves and Thornthwaite are simpler temperature-based methods.
Pan evaporation method: ETo = Kp × Epan (Class-A pan; pan coefficient ≈ 0.7).
Crop coefficient: ETcrop = Kc × ETo; Kc is low at the initial stage, maximum at mid-season (flowering), falls at maturity.
Available moisture = FC − PWP. Readily available moisture ≈ 75–80% of it. Irrigate before moisture falls to the readily-available limit.
Duty (D): area (hectares) irrigated by 1 cumec flowing continuously for the base period. Unit: ha/cumec.
Delta (Δ): total depth of water required by a crop during its base period (m or cm).
Base period (B): time between first and last watering before harvest (days).
Crop period: time from sowing to harvest (crop period ≥ base period; usually taken equal).
Relation: Δ = 8.64 B / D (Δ in m, B in days, D in ha/cumec).

Kor watering: first watering after crop grows a few cm; most critical. Kor depth (wheat ≈ 13.5 cm, rice ≈ 19 cm). Kor period: time in which kor watering must be done (wheat 3–4 weeks, rice 2–3 weeks).
Paleo: first watering before sowing to give moisture for germination.
Rice has the highest delta; wheat/fodder among lowest.
Type of crop, climate & season, rainfall, soil type, base period, method of irrigation, canal condition (lined/unlined), water quality, skill of cultivator.
Duty increases downstream due to losses: Duty at field > head of watercourse > head of distributary > head of main canal.
Improving duty: lining, proper ploughing, crop rotation, efficient methods (sprinkler/drip), volumetric water charges.
Gross command area (GCA): total area that can be irrigated by a canal, including roads, villages, ponds.
Culturable command area (CCA): GCA − unculturable area. CCA = culturable cultivated + culturable uncultivated.
Intensity of irrigation: % of CCA irrigated in a season. Can exceed 100% annually (e.g., Rabi + Kharif).
Time factor = days canal actually ran / days it was supposed to run.
Capacity factor = mean supply / full design supply.
Outlet factor: duty at the head of the watercourse (outlet).
Canal capacity: Q = (CCA × intensity) / duty, then adjusted for time factor & losses.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Given: Wheat: base period 120 days, delta 40 cm; CCA 10,000 ha; intensity 50%.
Area irrigated: 10,000 × 0.50 = 5000 ha → Q = 5000/2592 ≈ 1.93 cumec at the field (increase for losses at head).
Outlet factor (kor): Duty during kor period = 8.64 × kor period (days) / kor depth (m).
Kor periods (typical): Wheat ≈ 3–4 weeks (kor depth ≈ 13.5 cm); rice ≈ 2–3 weeks (kor depth ≈ 19 cm); sugarcane ≈ 4 weeks (≈ 16.5 cm).
Duty at field > duty at outlet > duty at head of canal (losses increase upstream). Rice has the highest delta (≈ 120 cm).
Salinity hazard: measured by Electrical Conductivity (EC). Classes C1 (low) to C4 (very high).
Sodium hazard: measured by SAR = Na⁺ / √[(Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺)/2] (meq/L). Classes S1 to S4.
Residual sodium carbonate (RSC) = (CO₃ + HCO₃) − (Ca + Mg); RSC > 2.5 meq/L unsuitable.
Boron: toxic above ~0.3–4 ppm depending on crop sensitivity.
Leaching requirement: LR = EC_iw / EC_dw (irrigation water EC / drainage water EC).
Definition: land is waterlogged when water table rises into root zone, reducing soil aeration & yield (rule of thumb: water table within ≈ 1.5–2 m of surface).
Causes: seepage from unlined canals, over-irrigation, poor natural drainage, obstruction of drainage by roads/railways, flat topography, impervious subsoil.
Effects: lack of aeration, fall in soil temperature, salt rise by capillarity (salinity), weed growth, malaria, reduced yield.

Remedies: canal lining, intercepting drains along canals, lowering FSL of canals, efficient irrigation, surface & subsurface drainage, vertical drainage by tube wells, crop rotation, reduced intensity.
SCARP (Pakistan): Salinity Control and Reclamation Project; began 1960s (SCARP-I in Rechna Doab); used tube wells for vertical drainage.
Surface drains: open ditches removing excess surface water.
Subsurface drains: tile/perforated pipe drains in trenches; spacing by Hooghoudt or ellipse equation S = √[4K(b² − a²)/q].
Tile drain min slope ≈ 0.05–0.3%; usual depth 1–2 m.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Waterlogging & salinity in Pakistan: Large areas of the Indus plains were affected by rising water tables after canal irrigation; SCARP tube wells (from 1960s), surface drains and the Left Bank Outfall Drain (LBOD) in Sindh were built to control it.
Reclamation of saline soil: Leaching with good-quality water + good drainage.
Reclamation of sodic (alkali) soil: Gypsum (CaSO₄) to replace Na⁺, followed by leaching; also sulphur, acid-forming amendments, organic matter.
Biological drainage: Eucalyptus and other high-transpiration trees planted to lower the water table.
Drain spacing: Hooghoudt’s equation is commonly used for spacing of subsurface drains.
Saline soil → leaching. Sodic soil → gypsum + leaching. SAR measures the sodium hazard; EC measures the salinity hazard.
By function: irrigation, carrier (irrigates + carries water to another canal), feeder (only feeds another canal), navigation, power canal.
By discharge/hierarchy: main canal → branch canal → major distributary → minor distributary → watercourse (field channel; farmer-owned).
Direct irrigation is normally not done from main canal; branch canals irrigate partly; distributaries feed outlets.

By alignment: (a) Watershed/ridge canal – runs along ridge; no cross-drainage works needed; irrigates both sides. (b) Contour canal – follows contour; irrigates one side; needs CD works. (c) Side-slope canal – perpendicular to contours; parallel to natural drainage; no CD works but steep slope (needs falls).
By soil: alluvial canal (in silt; design by regime theories), non-alluvial canal (hard soil/rock).
Full supply level (FSL): water level at full design discharge.
Freeboard: vertical distance between FSL and top of bank (≈ 0.3–0.9 m, depending on discharge).
Berm: horizontal strip between inner toe of bank and top of cutting; strengthens banks, protects from erosion; silt deposit forms 1/2:1 regime slope.
Balancing depth: depth of cutting at which earthwork in cutting = earthwork in filling (most economical).
Spoil bank: excess excavated earth dumped along canal. Borrow pit: pit dug to get earth for filling.
Service road / inspection road on bank top; dowla – small bank on road side for safety.
Seepage: major loss — (a) percolation (water table close; direct connection) and (b) absorption (water table deep; wetted zone only).
Typically 30–45% of diverted water may be lost in unlined systems.

Canal alignment types: Watershed (ridge) canal — no cross-drainage works, irrigates both sides; contour canal — irrigates one side, needs CD works; side-slope canal — at right angle to contours, parallel to drainage, no CD works but steep slope.
Berm functions: Strengthens banks, protects against erosion, room for future widening, deposit of silt forms lining (in time).
Seepage formulas: Losses in cumec per million m² of wetted area (e.g., ≈ 2.5 for unlined canals in Punjab practice).
Hierarchy in Pakistan: Main canal → branch canal → distributary (disty) → minor → watercourse (farmers’ channel) via outlet (mogha).
Balancing depth = depth of cutting for which cut = fill. Freeboard ≈ 0.5–0.75 m for main canals.
Based on observations on Upper Bari Doab Canal (UBDC), Punjab.
Silt kept in suspension by eddies generated from the bed only (sides ignored).
Critical velocity (V₀): velocity that neither silts nor scours: V₀ = 0.55 m D^0.64 (metric; D = depth of flow, m).
Critical velocity ratio (CVR, m) = V/V₀; m = 1 for UBDC silt; >1 for coarser silt, <1 for finer silt.
Mean velocity from Kutter's formula (later Manning's). Design by trial; Garret's diagrams used.
Limitations: no concept of silt charge or grade; B/D ratio not fixed; trial & error; Kutter's formula limitations; eddies from sides ignored.
Lindley first gave regime concept (1919); Lacey developed it fully.
Regime channel: neither silting nor scouring; bed & sides in equilibrium. Conditions: constant discharge, constant silt charge, incoherent alluvium of same grade, unlimited incoherent alluvium.
Types of regime: initial regime (bed slope & depth adjust, width fixed), final regime (all variables adjusted), true regime (theoretical ideal).
Silt supported by eddies generated from the entire wetted perimeter; normal to perimeter.
Regime section is a semi-ellipse; in practice trapezoidal with side slopes ½ : 1 (H:V).
Defects of Lacey: true regime rarely achieved; silt factor not truly constant; ignores silt concentration; semi-ellipse not practical; equations empirical.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Area, perimeter, R: A = Q/V ≈ 39 m²; P = 4.75√Q ≈ 26 m; R = 5V²/(2f) ≈ 1.48 m.
Kennedy’s CVR (m): m = 1.0 standard silt; coarser silt m > 1 (1.1–1.2); finer silt m < 1 (0.8–0.9).
Kennedy: eddies from the BED only keep silt in suspension; Lacey: eddies from the whole wetted PERIMETER. Lacey’s regime section ≈ semi-ellipse.

Advantages: seepage control (saves water), prevents waterlogging, higher velocity → smaller section, less maintenance, weed control, stable banks, better command (higher FSL possible), reduced breaches.
Disadvantages: high initial cost, repair is difficult, berms/outlets shifting difficult.
Hard surface: cement concrete (most common), shotcrete/gunite, brick/tile, stone masonry, asphalt concrete, precast slabs.
Earth type: compacted earth, soil–cement, bentonite/clay, buried membranes (plastic/asphalt).
Lined canal sections: triangular (small discharge, < ~55 cumec) and trapezoidal (larger discharge); corners rounded.
Uplift/hydrostatic pressure behind lining relieved by drainage: filter layers, pressure relief valves, longitudinal & cross drains.
Economics: Benefit–cost ratio = annual benefit / annual cost; lining justified if B/C > 1.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Concrete lining thickness: ≈ 75–100 mm for small canals, 100–150 mm for large canals; joints with bitumen/PVC water stops.
Brick-tile lining: Two layers of brick tiles in cement mortar — widely used in Pakistan for watercourses and small channels.
Pressure-relief: Drains/weep holes and pressure-release valves behind lining in high water-table areas.
Watercourse lining (Pakistan): On-Farm Water Management programmes line watercourses and laser-level fields to cut conveyance and field losses.
Benefits of lining: less seepage, no waterlogging, higher velocity (smaller section), less weed growth, lower maintenance.
Purpose: raise water level in river, divert into canal, regulate supply, control silt entry, reduce river fluctuation.
Weir: raised barrier across river; water level raised mainly by solid crest; shutters small/none. Pond level depends on crest.
Barrage: water level raised mainly by gates; crest at low level. Better control of pond level, silt and floods; costlier.
Weir/barrage proper – main body raising water level.
Undersluices (scouring sluices): deep pocket near canal head; keep channel clear of silt, provide still pond, scour silt.
Divide wall: separates undersluices from weir; creates still pocket; prevents cross flow.
Fish ladder: allows fish migration; located near divide wall.
Canal head regulator: controls supply into canal; excludes silt.
Silt excluder: in river bed upstream of head regulator; separates bottom silt-laden water.
Silt ejector (extractor): in canal downstream of head regulator; removes silt that already entered canal.
River training works: guide banks (Bell's bunds), marginal bunds, spurs/groynes.
Masonry weir with vertical drop wall; dry stone (rockfill) slope weir; concrete weir with sloping glacis (based on Khosla's theory; modern).

Pond level: Water level maintained upstream of weir/barrage for diversion into the canal.
Afflux: Rise in the high-flood level upstream caused by the weir/barrage; kept small (≈ 0.3–1.0 m).
Barrage advantages: Better control of pond level, less afflux, less silting, gates can be fully opened during floods.
Silt excluder is placed in the RIVER (upstream of the head regulator); silt ejector/extractor is placed in the CANAL (downstream of the head regulator).
Percolating water creeps along contact of base profile with soil (both vertical & horizontal equally).
Head loss is uniform (proportional to creep length) along path.
Creep length L = b + 2(d₁ + d₂ + …) (vertical cut-offs counted on both faces).
Hydraulic gradient = H_L / L; safe if H_L/L ≤ 1/C → L ≥ C · H_L (C = Bligh's creep coefficient).
Floor thickness: t = h / (G − 1); with safety factor t = (4/3) · h / (G − 1) (h = residual uplift head).
Limitations: no distinction between horizontal & vertical creep; exit gradient not considered; outer & inner faces of piles treated same; failed for some actual weirs.
Vertical creep given full weight; horizontal creep 1/3 weight: L = ΣL_v + (1/3) ΣL_h.
Slopes steeper than 45° → vertical; flatter than 45° → horizontal.
Based on potential flow theory (Laplace equation) & failures of Punjab weirs; flow net concept.
Outer faces of end sheet piles more effective than inner faces & floor.
Undermining starts at the tail end; a downstream end cut-off is essential to prevent piping.
Exit gradient must be within safe limit: G_E = (H/d) · 1/(π√λ), where λ = [1 + √(1 + α²)]/2, α = b/d.
Method of independent variables: complex profile split into simple standard profiles (pile at end, pile in middle, depressed floor); pressures φ_E, φ_D, φ_C found from Khosla's curves.
Corrections: (1) mutual interference of piles, (2) floor thickness, (3) slope of floor (+ for down slope, − for up slope).

Bligh: L = b + 2(d₁ + d₂); uniform head loss. Lane: horizontal creep counted as ⅓. Khosla: exit gradient GE = (H/d)·(1/π√λ) must be within safe limits.
Hydraulic jump: sudden rise of water when supercritical flow (F > 1) changes to subcritical flow (F < 1); dissipates energy.
Length of jump ≈ 5 to 7 × (y₂ − y₁) (≈ 6 × height of jump).
Energy dissipators: stilling basins (USBR Type I–IV, SAF), hydraulic jump basin, ski-jump (trajectory) bucket, roller bucket (solid/slotted), baffle blocks, chute blocks, end sill, friction blocks.
Ski-jump: used where tailwater is low & rock bed is good; roller bucket: tailwater depth high.

Fig. 10.1 — Hydraulic jump: y₁ (supercritical) → y₂ (subcritical), roller, length ≈ 6 (y₂ − y₁).
Uses of jump: Energy dissipation below spillways/falls, mixing of chemicals, raising d/s water level, aeration.
Tail-water rating curve: Jump forms at the toe only when tail-water depth = y₂; otherwise jump is repelled (TW < y₂) or drowned (TW > y₂).
Froude 4.5–9 = steady, well-balanced jump (best). F < 1.7 = undular; 2.5–4.5 = oscillating (avoid); > 9 = strong, rough.
Need: when natural ground slope is steeper than designed canal bed slope; bed lowered by a fall to avoid excessive filling.
Power can be generated at large falls.

Types: Ogee fall (old), rapids (long glacis, used where stone cheap), stepped fall, trapezoidal notch fall (Reid), vertical drop / Sarda fall (developed on Sarda canal, UP), straight glacis fall, Montague fall (parabolic glacis), Inglis fall (baffle wall), baffle fall, cylinder/well fall (high drop, small discharge), pipe fall.
Meter falls: used to measure discharge (e.g., glacis fall, notch fall). Non-meter falls: no measurement.
Head regulator: at head of off-taking canal; regulates supply into it; controls silt; can measure discharge.
Cross regulator: across parent canal just downstream of off-take; heads up water for off-take when parent canal runs low; helps close canal for repair; absorbs fluctuations.
Canal escape: disposes surplus water; types: weir type (surface), sluice type, tail escape (at end of canal).
Distributary head regulator = head regulator for distributary.
Canal outlet: small structure feeding watercourse from distributary.
Non-modular: discharge depends on difference of levels in distributary and watercourse (submerged pipe outlet, open sluice).

Semi-modular (flexible): discharge depends on distributary water level only, independent of watercourse level (free fall). Examples: pipe outlet with free fall, Kennedy's gauge outlet, open flume outlet, Crump's Adjustable Proportional Module (APM).
Modular (rigid): discharge constant within limits regardless of both levels. Examples: Gibb's module, Khanna's rigid module, Foote module.

F = 1 (outlet draws share proportional to distributary flow)
H/y = depth of outlet crest below FSL / full supply depth

Common falls: Sarda fall (vertical drop, UP/Sarda canal), straight glacis fall, Montague fall (parabolic glacis), Inglis fall, notch fall, pipe fall (small discharge), stepped fall.
Outlet terms: Flexibility = ratio of rate of change of outlet discharge to rate of change of distributary discharge; proportional outlet when flexibility = 1.
Rigid modules: Gibb’s module (most famous rigid module), Khanna’s rigid module; semi-modules — open flume, adjustable proportional module (APM, Crump).
Escapes: Tail escape (end of canal), surplus escape (weir/sluice type).
Head regulator is at the head of the off-taking channel; cross regulator is across the parent channel just d/s of the off-take.
Built where canal crosses a natural drain/stream. Avoided by watershed alignment.
Canal over drain; drain HFL well below canal bed; drain flows freely
Canal over drain; drain HFL above canal bed → drain flows under pressure (siphon action) below canal
Drain over canal; canal FSL below drain bed; canal flows freely
Drain over canal; canal FSL above drain bed → canal flows under pressure below drain
Canal & drain at nearly same level; large drain discharge; regulators on both
Small drain admitted into canal (inlet) and released (outlet)
Selection factors: relative bed levels & FSL/HFL, discharges, foundation, cost.
Aqueduct types: Type I – canal banks continued, drain waterway enclosed; Type II – canal sides as retaining walls; Type III – canal trough flumed (most economical).
Uplift on barrel floor of siphon aqueduct is critical (worst when drain empty & canal at FSL with water table high).

Level crossing: Canal and drain at about the same level; regulators on canal and drain; used when the drain discharge is large and short-duration.
Inlet & outlet: For small drains: drain water admitted into the canal (inlet) and released downstream (outlet).

Canal over drain (drain free) = aqueduct; canal over drain (drain under pressure) = siphon aqueduct; drain over canal (canal free) = super-passage; drain over canal (canal under pressure) = canal siphon.
By function: storage, diversion, detention (flood control), debris, coffer dam (temporary, to keep work area dry).
By material: rigid (concrete/masonry: gravity, arch, buttress) and non-rigid (earth, rockfill).
By hydraulic design: overflow (spillway) dam, non-overflow dam.
Resists water pressure by its own weight.
Forces: self weight (main resisting force), water pressure (main external force), uplift, silt pressure, wave pressure, ice pressure, earthquake forces (horizontal & vertical), wind.
Modes of failure: overturning, sliding, compression (crushing), tension (cracking).
No tension condition: resultant must lie within middle third of base (e ≤ b/6).
Elementary profile: right-angled triangle; base width b = H/√(S_c − c) with uplift (c = uplift coefficient); b = H/√S_c without uplift; for sliding b = H/[μ(S_c − c)].
Limiting height (low vs high dam): H = f / [γ_w (S_c + 1)] ≈ 88 m for usual concrete; dams higher than this = high gravity dams.
FOS against overturning = ΣM_R / ΣM_O (≥ 1.5). Sliding = μΣV/ΣH (≥ 1, usually 1–1.5). Shear friction factor = (μΣV + b·q)/ΣH (≥ 3–5).
Galleries: for inspection, drainage, grouting; drainage holes reduce uplift.
Types: homogeneous (single material; needs drainage), zoned (impervious core + pervious shells; most common), diaphragm (thin impervious diaphragm of concrete/steel/clay).

Causes of failure: (a) Hydraulic (≈ 40%) – overtopping (most common), wave erosion, toe erosion, gullying; (b) Seepage (≈ 30%) – piping, sloughing; (c) Structural (≈ 30%) – foundation slide, slope slide (u/s on sudden drawdown, d/s at steady seepage), earthquake.
Phreatic line: top seepage line; approximately a base parabola (Casagrande) with focus at toe of filter/drain.
Seepage discharge (flow net): q = k H (N_f / N_d).
Seepage control: impervious core, cut-off trench, grouted curtain, upstream impervious blanket, relief wells.
Drainage filters: toe filter / rock toe, horizontal blanket, chimney drain.
Critical conditions for stability: u/s slope – sudden drawdown; d/s slope – steady seepage; both – construction (end of construction pore pressure).
Arch dam: curved in plan, transfers load to abutments by arch action; narrow gorge with strong rock (width/height < ~5). Constant-radius, constant-angle (most economical), variable radius.
Buttress dam: sloping deck supported by buttresses; less concrete; types: deck (Ambursen), multiple arch, massive head.
Rockfill dam: rock with impervious membrane (concrete face – CFRD) or core.
Narrow valley with wide basin upstream, sound foundation, availability of materials, spillway site, low land acquisition/submergence, minimal sediment, access, cost.

Principal stresses: Maximum principal stress occurs at the toe; minimum (possible tension) at the heel.
Earth dam piping: Prevented by filters (Terzaghi’s criteria), cut-offs, relief wells and adequate seepage path.

Spillway: passes surplus flood water safely to downstream; prevents overtopping.

Primed by air removal; automatic, maintains near-constant level; limited capacity
Closed conduit through or around dam
Cavitation: occurs if pressure falls below vapour pressure (negative pressure on crest when head > design head).
Gates: vertical lift (fixed wheel, slide), radial (Tainter) gate – most common on spillways/barrages, drum gate, rolling gate, stop logs, needles, flash boards.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Spillway types: Free overfall (straight drop), ogee (most common), chute/trough, side-channel (narrow valleys), shaft/morning-glory (bell-mouth), siphon (automatic, constant pool), labyrinth/piano-key.
Spillway capacity: Designed for the inflow design flood after routing through the reservoir (PMF for large dams).
Aerators: Slots/ramps on chute surface introduce air to prevent cavitation at high velocities.
Ogee crest profile follows the lower nappe of a sharp-crested weir (WES standard shape).

chapters.t: Gravity Dam — Design Checks & Worked Example
b: Forces (per metre length): Self-weight W (main stabilising force), water pressure P = ½γwH² at H/3, uplift U = ½·c·γw·H·B (c = 1 without drains; reduced with drainage gallery), silt pressure, wave pressure, ice, earthquake (horizontal & vertical inertia + Zangar/Westergaard hydrodynamic pressure).

Elementary profile: Triangle with zero top width and vertical upstream face, height H, base B. No tension (resultant in middle third): B ≥ H/√(Sc − c); without uplift B = H/√Sc. Sliding: B ≥ H/[μ(Sc − c)].
Stability checks: Overturning FOS = ΣMR/ΣMO ≥ 1.5; sliding FOS = μΣV/ΣH ≥ 1.0–1.5; shear-friction factor SFF = (μΣV + B·q)/ΣH ≥ 3–5; no tension (e ≤ B/6); compressive stress ≤ allowable.
Base pressures: p = (ΣV/B)(1 ± 6e/B); e = B/2 − x̄, where x̄ = (ΣMR − ΣMO)/ΣV measured from the toe.
Load combinations (USBR): Usual (normal pool + uplift + silt + ice), unusual (maximum flood), extreme (usual + maximum credible earthquake).
Fig. — Forces on the elementary profile of the worked example: water pressure, self-weight, uplift and resultant in the middle third.
Given: H = 30 m, B = 26 m, vertical upstream face, γc = 24 kN/m³, γw = 9.81 kN/m³, full uplift (c = 1, triangular), μ = 0.75; reservoir full to the top.

Forces: W = ½ × 26 × 30 × 24 = 9,360 kN (acts B/3 = 8.67 m from heel → 17.33 m from toe). P = ½ × 9.81 × 30² = 4,414.5 kN at 10 m. U = ½ × 9.81 × 30 × 26 = 3,825.9 kN at B/3 from heel (17.33 m from toe).
Sliding: FOS = 0.75 × 5,534 / 4,414.5 = 0.94 < 1 → unsafe by pure friction; needs shear-key / bond (SFF check), a wider base (B ≥ H/[μ(Sc − c)] = 28.6 m) or drainage to cut uplift.
Uplift is what makes the elementary profile fail in sliding — drainage galleries and grout curtains reduce c and are the cheapest fix.
Types: Homogeneous (with toe drain/filter), zoned (impervious core + pervious shells — most common for high dams; Tarbela, Mangla), diaphragm (thin core of concrete/asphalt).

Phreatic line (Casagrande / Kozeny): Basic parabola with focus at the start of the toe filter: y² = 2xy₀ + y₀², y₀ = √(h² + d²) − d (h = water depth, d = horizontal distance from focus to the point 0.3 × upstream wetted projection). Seepage q = k·y₀ per metre.
Seepage by flow net: q = k·h·(Nf/Nd) per metre length (Nf = flow channels, Nd = equipotential drops).
Fig. — Zoned earth dam: impervious core, pervious shells, chimney filter and drain; the phreatic line ends in the filter.
Critical conditions: Upstream slope — sudden drawdown; downstream slope — steady seepage at full reservoir; both slopes — end of construction (pore pressure).
Failures: Hydraulic (overtopping, wave erosion, toe erosion, gullies); seepage (piping, sloughing); structural (slides, foundation shear, earthquake). Freeboard prevents overtopping.
Typical slopes: Upstream 2.5H:1V–3H:1V (flatter, drawdown), downstream 2H:1V–2.5H:1V; top width (USBR) = H/5 + 3 m (H in m) or empirical.
Upstream slope is critical in sudden drawdown; downstream slope in steady seepage. Phreatic line meets the downstream filter — never the slope face.
Ogee spillway discharge: Q = C·L·He^(3/2); C ≈ 2.2 (SI) at design head (≈ 4.0 in ft-units). Effective length L = L′ − 2(N·Kp + Ka)He (pier & abutment contractions).
WES crest profile (vertical upstream face): x^1.85 = 2·Hd^0.85·y (downstream of crest).

Hydraulic jump in stilling basins (USBR): Fr₁ 1.7–2.5: no baffles (pre-jump); 2.5–4.5: oscillating jump → Type IV basin; Fr₁ > 4.5 with V₁ < 18 m/s → Type III (chute blocks, baffle piers, end sill); V₁ > 18 m/s → Type II (no baffle piers).
Fig. — Ogee spillway discharging into a USBR Type III stilling basin with chute blocks, baffle piers and end sill.
Other dissipators: Roller bucket (solid / slotted) where tail water is high; ski-jump / flip bucket where tail water is low and rock is sound; plunge pool.
Spillway design flood: Large dams → PMF (probable maximum flood); medium → 100–1000-yr flood; check freeboard against wave run-up.

Outlets & gates: Low-level outlets/sluices for irrigation and sediment flushing; radial (Tainter) gates (least hoisting force, most common on spillways); vertical lift gates; stop logs for maintenance.
Ski-jump bucket = low tail water; roller bucket = high tail water; hydraulic-jump basin = tail water matching sequent depth.
Power: P = η·γw·Q·H = 9.81·η·Q·H kW (Q in m³/s, H = net head in m). Energy (kWh) = P × hours. Overall η ≈ 0.80–0.90.
Worked example: Q = 100 m³/s, Hnet = 80 m, η = 0.88 → P = 9.81 × 0.88 × 100 × 80 = 69,062 kW ≈ 69 MW. Annual energy at 50% capacity factor ≈ 69 × 8760 × 0.5 ≈ 302 GWh.
Heads: Gross head = headwater − tailwater level; net (effective) head = gross − losses (trash rack, intake, penstock friction, bends, valves).

Classification by head (Garg): Low head < 15 m (Kaplan/propeller/bulb), medium 15–60 m (Francis, Kaplan), high > 60 m (Pelton, Francis). Other books use < 30 m / 30–300 m / > 300 m — note the book used in the paper.

Classification by operation: Run-of-river without pondage, run-of-river with pondage (daily regulation), storage (seasonal), pumped storage (peak-load; pumps at off-peak, generates at peak; cycle efficiency ≈ 70–80%), tidal.
Classification by load: Base-load plants (large storage & run-of-river with steady flow) vs peak-load plants (pumped storage, pondage plants).

Components: Reservoir/headworks → intake with trash rack → headrace (tunnel/canal) → forebay (open-channel systems) or surge tank (pressure systems) → penstock → powerhouse (turbine, generator, governor) → draft tube (reaction turbines) → tailrace.
Fig. — Layout of a high-head scheme: intake, headrace tunnel, surge tank, penstock, powerhouse, draft tube and tailrace.

Surge tank: Absorbs water-hammer pressure rise on load rejection and supplies water on sudden load demand; protects the headrace tunnel. Types: simple, restricted-orifice, differential (Johnson), closed (air cushion).
Water hammer: Joukowsky pressure rise Δp = ρ·c·ΔV for rapid closure (closure time < 2L/c); slow closure reduces it. Wave speed c ≈ 1000–1400 m/s in steel penstocks.

Penstock: Steel (most common), RCC (low head), wood-stave (old). Economical diameter balances friction loss against cost; velocity ≈ 3–7 m/s (higher for higher heads). Anchor blocks at bends; expansion joints between anchors.

Draft tube: Diverging tube from runner exit to tailrace — recovers kinetic energy and allows turbine above tailwater. Types: conical (straight divergent, η ≈ 90%), elbow, Moody spreading, simple elbow. Not used with Pelton (impulse) wheels.
Cavitation: Thoma coefficient σ = (Ha − Hv − Hs)/H; must exceed σc of the runner. Hs = suction head (runner above tailwater). Reaction turbines (Francis, Kaplan) are prone; Pelton is not.

Turbine selection by head (approx.): Pelton (impulse) ≈ 250–1800 m; Francis ≈ 40–600 m; Kaplan/propeller ≈ 2–70 m; bulb turbines for very low heads (< 20 m). Specific speed rises from Pelton → Francis → Kaplan.
P (kW) = 9.81 η Q H. Surge tank → water hammer protection of the tunnel; draft tube → regains velocity head, used only with reaction turbines.
Load factor: Average load ÷ peak load over a period (always < 1).
Fig. — Daily load curve: peak demand 100 MW, average ≈ 65 MW, so load factor ≈ 0.65.
Capacity (plant) factor: Average output ÷ installed capacity = actual energy ÷ (installed capacity × hours).
Utilisation (plant use) factor: Actual energy produced ÷ (capacity actually used × hours) — always ≥ capacity factor.
Diversity factor: Sum of individual maximum demands ÷ maximum demand of the system (≥ 1).
Firm (primary) power: Power available at all times (based on minimum flow, or 90–95% dependable flow). Secondary (surplus) power — available only part of the time; sold at lower rates.
Flow-duration curve: Discharge vs % time equalled or exceeded — used to fix firm power and installed capacity of run-of-river plants. Power-duration curve = same with power ordinate.
Mass curve / sequent-peak: Storage required for a given demand (Rippl method) — used for storage plants.
Pondage factor: Total inflow hours in a period ÷ hours of plant operation in the same period.
Load factor = average/peak demand; capacity factor = average output/installed capacity. Firm power is fixed from the minimum (or 90–95% dependable) flow.
Earth & rock-fill; 4th ext. 1,410 MW (2018); 5th ext. +1,530 MW under construction → 6,418
RCC dam ≈ 272 m high, storage ≈ 8.1 MAF, under construction
CFRD; flood control + water supply, under construction
Pakistan hydropower share: Total installed capacity ≈ 49,000+ MW (2024), of which ≈ 11,500 MW hydro; identified potential ≈ 60,000 MW (mostly the Indus cascade in KP & GB).
Tarbela is the largest hydropower station of Pakistan (4,888 MW); Ghazi-Barotha and Neelum–Jhelum are run-of-river; Diamer-Bhasha is designed as an RCC (roller-compacted concrete) dam.
Dead storage: below minimum pool level; for silt; cannot be released by gravity.
Live (useful) storage: between minimum pool level and normal pool (conservation) level.
Surcharge storage: between normal pool level and maximum pool level (flood storage; uncontrolled).
Bank storage: water absorbed into banks; valley storage: natural river channel storage before dam.
Mass curve (Rippl) method: used to find required storage capacity / safe yield.
Safe (firm) yield: max quantity guaranteed in critical dry period. Secondary yield: water available in excess of safe yield.
Reservoir sedimentation: trap efficiency depends on capacity–inflow ratio (Brune's curve). Life of reservoir = time to fill dead storage (or capacity reduced to set %).
Control of silting: catchment treatment (afforestation, check dams), sluicing, flushing, venting density currents, dredging, selecting site with low sediment.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 21.1 — Reservoir storage zones: dead, live (useful) and surcharge storage; minimum, normal and maximum pool levels.
Trap efficiency: Brune’s curve — trap efficiency vs capacity/inflow ratio; large reservoirs trap ≈ 90–100% of sediment.
Sediment in Pakistan reservoirs: Tarbela and Mangla have lost a significant part of their original storage to sediment, a key reason for new storages.
Life of reservoir: Usually taken as the time until ≈ 50–80% of capacity is silted (depends on purpose).
Mass curve (Rippl) method gives the storage needed for a given demand; the maximum ordinate between demand line tangents = required storage.

b: Storage zones: Dead storage (below minimum drawdown — sediment), live/useful storage (between MDDL & normal pool), flood storage/surcharge (between normal pool and maximum water level), freeboard above MWL.
Mass curve (Rippl) method: Storage required = maximum cumulative deficiency between demand line and inflow mass curve; sequent-peak algorithm for computation.
Reservoir sedimentation: Trap efficiency vs capacity/inflow ratio (Brune's curve); Tarbela & Mangla losing live storage to silt — reason for raising Mangla (2009) and for new dams.
Yield: Firm (safe) yield — guaranteed in the critical dry period; secondary yield — available in wetter years.
Mass-curve method: draw demand lines tangent at the peaks of the inflow mass curve — the largest vertical gap to the next trough = required storage.
Rivers by stage: rocky/mountain (incised), boulder, alluvial (trough), tidal/delta.
Alluvial rivers: aggrading (silting), degrading (scouring), meandering (single sinuous channel), braided (multiple channels, wide shallow).
Meander ratio = meander belt / meander length. Tortuosity = curved length / straight length (> 1).
Objectives of training: high flood protection, safe passage of flood, sediment control, navigable depth, stable course near structures.
Guide banks (Bell's bunds): confine river to approach bridge/barrage; length ≈ 1.1–1.5 × Lacey's waterway u/s, 0.1–0.25 d/s.
Marginal embankments / levees: parallel to river to prevent spill.
Groynes / spurs: transverse structures. Attracting spur points downstream, repelling spur points upstream, deflecting spur is perpendicular & short.
Pitching & launching apron: stone protection of slopes; apron settles into scour hole.
Artificial cut-offs: shorten meander loops. Pitched islands, bank revetment, closure dykes.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)

Lacey’s scour depth: R = 0.47 (Q/f)^(1/3); maximum scour depth below HFL ≈ 1.25R (straight reach), 1.5R (moderate bend), 1.75R (severe bend), 2R (right-angled bend); larger (≈ 2–2.75R) at noses of guide banks/spurs.
Guide bank length: Upstream ≈ 1.0–1.5 × waterway length; downstream ≈ 0.25 × waterway (Spring’s/Gales’ practice).
Spur types (by action): Attracting (points d/s), deflecting (normal to flow), repelling (points u/s); also by construction — permeable / impermeable, submerged / non-submerged.
Repelling spur points UPSTREAM and pushes the river away; attracting spur points DOWNSTREAM and attracts the river towards the bank.
Aquifer: stores & transmits water (sand, gravel). Aquitard: stores, transmits slowly (sandy clay). Aquiclude: stores, does not transmit (clay). Aquifuge: neither (solid rock).

Unconfined (water table) aquifer: upper surface at atmospheric pressure. Confined (artesian): between impervious layers; under pressure. Perched aquifer: above main water table on local impervious lens.
Storage coefficient: volume released per unit area per unit head decline (confined: 10⁻⁵–10⁻³; unconfined ≈ specific yield).
Transmissivity T = K·b (b = aquifer thickness). Darcy's law: V = K i; valid for laminar flow (Re < 1).
Open wells: shallow (in unconfined aquifer) / deep; yield by recuperation test; specific capacity.
Tube wells: strainer type, cavity type, slotted type; well development removes fines around screen; gravel pack well.
Cone of depression, radius of influence, drawdown – key well terms.
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Specific capacity: Well discharge per unit drawdown (m³/day per m).
Pumping tests: Theis (non-equilibrium), Jacob’s straight-line method, recovery test — give T and S.
Well development: Surging, back-washing, over-pumping, compressed air — removes fines and increases yield.
Interference: Overlapping cones of depression reduce yields of nearby wells; maintain spacing ≥ ≈ 2 × radius of influence.
Confined aquifer storage coefficient ≈ 10⁻⁵–10⁻³; unconfined ≈ specific yield (≈ 0.05–0.3).

b: Aquifer types: Aquifer (stores & yields), aquitard (leaky, low permeability), aquiclude (stores but does not transmit — clay), aquifuge (neither — solid granite).

Confined vs unconfined: Unconfined: water table at atmospheric pressure; confined (artesian): between impermeable layers, piezometric surface above top; flowing well if piezometric surface is above ground.
Properties: Porosity n, specific yield Sy (+ specific retention Sr = n), storativity S (confined ≈ 10⁻⁵–10⁻³; unconfined ≈ Sy), transmissivity T = K b.
Darcy's law: Q = K i A; valid for laminar flow (Re < 1–10).
Steady well flow (Thiem/Dupuit): Confined: Q = 2πKb(h₂ − h₁)/ln(r₂/r₁); unconfined: Q = πK(h₂² − h₁²)/ln(r₂/r₁).
Unsteady (Theis): s = Q W(u)/(4πT), u = r²S/(4Tt); Cooper–Jacob approximation for u < 0.01.
Pakistan: Indus Basin aquifer is one of the largest in the world; over-pumping lowers water tables (Lahore, Quetta). Waterlogging & salinity tackled by SCARP tubewells.
Specific yield + specific retention = porosity. Cone of depression extends to the radius of influence R.
One of the largest contiguous gravity irrigation systems in the world.
Indus Waters Treaty: signed 19 Sept 1960 in Karachi between Pakistan (Ayub Khan) and India (Nehru), brokered by World Bank.
Eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) → India. Western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) → Pakistan.
Indus Basin Project (replacement works): Mangla Dam (Jhelum, 1967), Tarbela Dam (Indus, 1976; one of world's largest earth/rockfill dams), 5 barrages, 1 siphon and 8 link canals.
System has 3 major reservoirs (Tarbela, Mangla, Chashma), 12 inter-river link canals, ~45 canal commands and 100,000+ watercourses.
Water Apportionment Accord: 1991 (between provinces). IRSA (Indus River System Authority) set up 1992 to implement it.
Jinnah (Kalabagh), Chashma, Taunsa, Guddu, Sukkur, Kotri (Ghulam Muhammad)
Sukkur Barrage (1932): formerly Lloyd Barrage; feeds 7 canals; among the largest single barrage irrigation systems.
Panjnad: confluence of five eastern/central rivers before joining Indus.
Other dams: Warsak (Kabul River), Hub Dam, Khanpur Dam (Haro River), Rawal Dam (Korang), Simly Dam; Diamer-Bhasha & Mohmand dams (under construction).

Fig. 24.1 — Schematic of the Indus Basin rivers with main dams and barrages (not to scale).
New storages (2026): WAPDA is executing Mohmand Dam (Swat River), Tarbela 5th Extension, Diamer-Bhasha Dam and the Dasu Hydropower Project, besides the K-IV Karachi water scheme.
Diamer-Bhasha Dam: ≈ 272 m high — the highest RCC dam in the world; gross storage ≈ 8.1 MAF; ≈ 4,500 MW; Indus diverted in December 2023; still under construction.
Dasu Hydropower Project: 4,320 MW run-of-river project on the Indus, built in two stages; river diverted in February 2023.
Mohmand Dam: Concrete-face rockfill dam on the Swat River; ≈ 1.2–1.29 MAF storage, 800 MW; flood relief for Peshawar, Charsadda and Nowshera; completion expected around 2027-28.
Tarbela extensions: 4th and 5th extensions raise installed capacity from 4,888 MW to 6,418 MW.

Indus Waters Treaty — 2025: On 23 April 2025 India announced it was holding the treaty ‘in abeyance’; Pakistan rejected the move, stating the treaty has no provision for unilateral suspension (World Bank-brokered, 1960). Keep track of current developments before the exam.
Western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) → Pakistan; Eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) → India (Indus Waters Treaty, 1960).
Duty is expressed in ha/cumec; delta in cm or m.
Kennedy's theory based on Upper Bari Doab Canal.
Bligh: horizontal and vertical creep given equal weight.
Khosla: failure (piping) starts at downstream end — d/s cut-off essential.
Cross regulator is built in the parent canal d/s of off-take.
Gibb's module is a rigid module; open flume is semi-modular.
Drain over canal with canal running free: super passage.
Sarda fall is a vertical drop type fall.
Gravity dam no-tension: resultant in middle third.
Most common cause of earth dam failure: overtopping.
Phreatic line in earth dam: base parabola (Casagrande).
U/s slope of earth dam critical during sudden drawdown.
Most common spillway in gravity dams: ogee.
Spillway with automatic action and constant pool: siphon spillway.
Most accurate method of average rainfall: isohyetal.
Saline soil: EC > 4 dS/m, ESP < 15, pH < 8.5.

Manning’s equation: V = (1/n) R^(2/3) S^(1/2); most economical trapezoidal section is half a hexagon (R = y/2).
Most economical rectangular section: Width = 2 × depth; R = y/2.
Duty = ha/cumec (area); delta = depth of water (cm/m)
Base period ≤ crop period (first to last watering vs sowing to harvest)
Paleo = pre-sowing; kor = first watering after crop is a few cm high (largest)
Weir: water raised by crest/shutters; barrage: raised mainly by gates, crest low
Excluder: river, u/s of head regulator; ejector: canal, d/s of head regulator

Fig. 28.1 — The hydrologic cycle: precipitation, interception, infiltration, runoff, evaporation and transpiration.
Hydrology: Science of the occurrence, circulation and distribution of water on Earth; engineering hydrology deals with estimating design flows, yields and storages.
Water budget: P − R − G − E − T = ΔS (precipitation − runoff − groundwater outflow − evaporation − transpiration = change in storage).
Catchment (watershed / drainage basin): Area draining to a single outlet, bounded by the water divide (ridge line).
Global distribution: ≈ 97% of Earth's water is in oceans; ≈ 2% in ice caps/glaciers; < 1% is fresh liquid water (mostly groundwater).
Applications: Design floods for spillways, bridges, culverts and drains; reservoir capacity; irrigation & water-supply yield; flood forecasting; drought studies.
Residence time: atmosphere ≈ 8–10 days, rivers ≈ 2 weeks, oceans ≈ 3,000+ years, deep groundwater ≈ up to 10,000 years.

s.t: More on this topic — Irrigation Engineering: Hydrology (Brief)
b: Hydrological cycle: evaporation → condensation → precipitation → infiltration/runoff → back to sea.
Rain gauges: non-recording – Symon's gauge; recording – tipping bucket, weighing bucket, float (natural siphon) type.
Average rainfall: arithmetic mean (flat, uniform), Thiessen polygon (weights by area), isohyetal (most accurate).
Infiltration: Horton's equation f = f_c + (f₀ − f_c) e^(−kt); φ-index (avg rate above which rainfall = runoff); W-index.
Rational formula: Q = CIA/3.6 (Q m³/s, I mm/h, A km²); for small catchments.
Hydrograph: rising limb, crest (peak), recession limb; base flow + direct runoff.
Unit hydrograph (Sherman, 1932): hydrograph of 1 cm direct runoff from rain of unit duration uniformly over catchment. S-curve used to change duration.
Flood routing: reservoir – Modified Puls / Goodrich method; channel – Muskingum method.
Return period: T = 1/P. Risk: R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ over n years. Gumbel's method for flood frequency.
Design floods: PMF (probable maximum flood) for large dams; SPF (standard project flood).
Extended material (beyond the lectures — standard textbooks & online sources)
Fig. 28.2 — Flood hydrograph: rising limb, crest, recession limb, base flow and direct runoff.
Runoff estimation: Rational formula (small catchments), Dickens / Ryves (empirical), unit hydrograph (medium), SCS-CN method (curve number).
S-curve: Used to change the duration of a unit hydrograph.
Network design: Minimum gauges & optimum number by coefficient of variation: N = (Cv/ε)².
Flood frequency: Gumbel’s extreme-value method; Log-Pearson Type III; California method T = n/m (Weibull: T = (n + 1)/m).
φ-index = average infiltration rate above which rainfall volume = runoff volume; W-index excludes initial losses.
Forms: Rain (> 0.5 mm drops), drizzle (< 0.5 mm, intensity < 1 mm/h), snow, sleet, hail (> 8 mm ice balls), glaze.

Types by lifting mechanism: Convective (local heating, thunderstorms), orographic (forced over mountains — monsoon in northern Pakistan), cyclonic/frontal (warm & cold fronts; western disturbances in winter).
Non-recording gauge: Symon's (standard) gauge — 127 mm funnel, read daily at 8:30 AM (IMD/PMD practice).
Recording gauges: Tipping-bucket (0.25 mm buckets, electronic pulses), weighing-bucket (records snow too), natural-siphon/float (Hellmann) — give the mass curve and intensity.
Gauge siting: Distance from obstruction ≥ 2 × its height (preferably 4×); level ground, fenced enclosure.
Optimum number of gauges: N = (Cv/ε)², Cv = coefficient of variation of existing gauge records, ε = allowable error (%; usually 10%).
Missing data: Arithmetic mean if normal annual rainfalls differ < 10%; otherwise normal-ratio method: Px = (Nx/n) Σ(Pi/Ni).
Consistency check: Double-mass curve: cumulative station rainfall vs cumulative group mean; a break in slope shows a change (correct by slope ratio).
Mean areal rainfall: Arithmetic mean (flat, dense network); Thiessen polygon (area-weighted, most common); Isohyetal (most accurate, uses orography).
DAD curves: Depth–Area–Duration: average depth decreases exponentially with area for a given duration (P = P₀ e^(−kAⁿ)).
Fig. 29.1 — Intensity–Duration–Frequency curves: intensity falls with duration and rises with return period.
IDF models: i = K Tˣ / (t + a)ⁿ (Sherman); Talbot i = a/(t + b); Kirpich/Bernard forms. Coefficients fitted by log-linear regression of observed intensities (as in the CE-323 final paper).
Thiessen = area-weighted; Isohyetal = most accurate; Double-mass curve = consistency; Normal-ratio = missing record when normals differ > 10%.
Evaporation factors: Vapour-pressure difference (Dalton's law E = C(ew − ea)), temperature, wind, atmospheric pressure, dissolved salts (salinity reduces evaporation).
Measurement: Class-A pan (USWB, 1210 mm dia, 255 mm deep); pan coefficient ≈ 0.7 (lake evaporation = 0.7 × pan). Colorado sunken pan coefficient ≈ 0.78.
Evaporation reduction: Cetyl alcohol (hexadecanol) monomolecular films, wind breaks, floating covers, reducing surface area.
Evapotranspiration: PET (water not limiting) vs AET; estimated by Penman / Penman–Monteith (FAO-56), Blaney–Criddle, Thornthwaite, Hargreaves; measured with lysimeters.
Infiltration: Entry of water into soil surface; percolation = downward movement below the root zone. Infiltration capacity fc depends on soil type, moisture, cover, compaction and temperature.
Horton equation: f = fc + (f₀ − fc) e^(−kt) — capacity decays exponentially to a constant rate.
Other models: Philip: F = S t½ + K t; Green–Ampt (physically based); Kostiakov.
Infiltration indices: φ-index = constant rate above which rainfall volume = runoff volume; W-index = φ excluding initial losses (W ≤ φ).
Measurement: Double-ring (flooding) infiltrometer — outer ring prevents lateral spreading; rainfall simulators.
φ-index: rainfall above φ = runoff. For a storm, total rain − runoff = losses; find φ by trial so that Σ(i − φ)·Δt = runoff depth.
Stage: Water-surface elevation; measured by staff gauge, wire gauge, float recorder, bubble gauge, radar/pressure sensor.
Area–velocity method: Q = Σ (a_i v_i). Current meter (cup type — Price; propeller type) with rating V = a N + b (N = revolutions/time).
Velocity sampling: Single point at 0.6 d (shallow, < 3 m) or mean of 0.2 d & 0.8 d (deep). Surface velocity × 0.85 ≈ mean velocity.
Section computation: Mid-section method or mean-section method; segments should carry ≤ 10% of total discharge.
Other methods: Float method (rough), dilution/tracer (mountain streams), ultrasonic (ADCP), electromagnetic, slope-area (Manning) for past floods, weirs & flumes (Parshall) for small channels.
Rating curve: Stage–discharge relation Q = Cr (G − a)^β fitted by log regression; extended by log-log or Stevens method; loop rating under unsteady flow.
Mean velocity ≈ velocity at 0.6 depth from surface ≈ average of velocities at 0.2 d and 0.8 d.
Fig. 32.1 — Components of a flood hydrograph and base-flow separation.
Runoff components: Surface (overland) flow, interflow (subsurface storm flow) and base flow (groundwater). Direct runoff = surface + prompt interflow.
Stream types: Perennial (always flows — base flow), intermittent (flows in wet season), ephemeral (only after storms; arid areas).
Hydrograph parts: Rising limb (concentration curve), crest/peak, falling limb (recession), inflection point (end of direct-runoff inflow).
Base-flow separation: Straight-line method; fixed-base length N = 0.83 A^0.2 (N in days, A in km²); variable-slope method.

Factors affecting shape: Climatic (intensity, duration, storm movement — storms moving downstream give higher peaks) and physiographic (area, shape — fan-shaped basins give sharp peaks, slope, drainage density, land use).
Time of concentration tc: Time for runoff from the hydraulically most remote point to reach the outlet. Kirpich: tc = 0.01947 L^0.77 S^−0.385 (min; L in m, S in m/m).
Rational method: Qp = C i A / 3.6 (Qp m³/s, i mm/h, A km²) or Q = 0.278 C i A; i for duration = tc; for small catchments (< 50 km², urban drains, culverts).
Fig. 32.2 — SCS-CN runoff equation for different curve numbers.

SCS Curve Number: Q = (P − 0.2S)² / (P + 0.8S) for P > 0.2S; S = 25400/CN − 254 (mm). CN depends on hydrologic soil group (A–D), land use/cover and antecedent moisture (AMC I dry, II normal, III wet).
Rational formula: Q = CiA/360 with A in hectares (Q m³/s, i mm/h). CN = 100 → all rain becomes runoff; higher CN → more runoff.
Definition: D-h unit hydrograph: DRH from 1 cm (or 1 mm/1 inch) of effective rainfall uniformly distributed over the basin in D hours (Sherman, 1932).
Assumptions: Time invariance and linear response — principle of proportionality (ordinates ∝ rainfall excess) and superposition; uniform rainfall in space and time.
Derivation: Separate base flow → DRH; effective rain depth = DRH volume / area; UH ordinates = DRH ordinates / effective depth.
Volume check: Σ UH ordinates × Δt = 1 cm × A → for 1-cm UH: Σ Q (m³/s) × Δt (h) × 0.36 = A (km²).
Multiple storms: Successive storms: lag and add (superposition); complex storms: matrix method or successive subtraction (as in the CE-323 final paper: UH3 from three 3-h storms).
Fig. 33.1 — S-curve method to change unit-hydrograph duration.
Changing duration: Lagging method if T = n·D (add n UHs lagged by D, divide by n); S-curve method for any T: UH_T = (S(t) − S(t − T)) × D/T.
S-curve equilibrium discharge: Qe = 2.778 A / D (Qe m³/s, A km², D h).
IUH: Instantaneous unit hydrograph: D → 0; Nash model (cascade of n linear reservoirs), Clark model (time-area + linear reservoir).
To convert UH3 to UH6: lagging method works (6 = 2 × 3); add UH3 and UH3 lagged by 3 h, divide by 2.
Need: Ungauged catchments — UH derived from basin characteristics.
Snyder (1938): Basin lag tp = Ct (L·Lc)^0.3 (h; L, Lc in km, Ct 1.35–1.65); peak Qp = 2.78 Cp A / tp; standard duration tr = tp/5.5; base T = 3 + 3(tp/24) days.
SCS dimensionless UH: tp = D/2 + tlag; tlag ≈ 0.6 tc; Qp = 2.08 A / tp (A km², tp h, Qp m³/s per cm); base ≈ 2.67 tp (triangular).
Others: Gray, Espey, Clark time-area method, geomorphological IUH.
SCS triangular UH: time base = 2.67 tp, recession = 1.67 tp; peak factor 484 (US units) ↔ 2.08 (SI with A in km²).
Return period: T = 1/P; probability of at least one exceedance in n years: R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ (risk). Reliability = (1 − 1/T)ⁿ.
Plotting position: Weibull: T = (N + 1)/m (m = rank in descending order).
Gumbel (EV-I): K = −(√6/π)[0.5772 + ln ln(T/(T − 1))]; reduced variate y = −ln ln(T/(T − 1)); for finite N use ȳn, Sn tables.
Log-Pearson Type III: Used in US (Bulletin 17C); applied to log Q with skew coefficient.
Empirical formulas: Dickens Q = C A^¾; Ryves Q = C A^⅔; Inglis Q = 124 A/√(A + 10.4) (A km²).
Design floods: Spillways of major dams — PMF (probable maximum flood); barrages/major bridges — 100–1000-yr flood; culverts — 25–50 yr; urban drains — 2–10 yr.
PMP: Probable maximum precipitation — by storm maximisation/transposition or Hershfield statistical method (K ≈ 15).
Risk of a 100-yr flood being exceeded at least once in 100 years = 1 − 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 63%.
Fig. 36.1 — Reservoir routing: peak attenuation and lag; the outflow peak occurs where outflow equals inflow.
Purpose: Determine the outflow hydrograph at a downstream point from the inflow hydrograph — attenuation (peak reduction) and translation (lag).
Continuity: I − O = dS/dt → ((I₁ + I₂)/2)Δt − ((O₁ + O₂)/2)Δt = S₂ − S₁.
Reservoir (level-pool) routing: Modified Puls / storage-indication: (2S₂/Δt + O₂) = (I₁ + I₂) + (2S₁/Δt − O₁); Goodrich method.
Linear reservoir: S = K O → O₂ = C₁ I₁ + C₂ I₂ + C₃ O₁ with routing coefficients from K and Δt (CE-323 final: K = 2 h, Δt = 1 h).

Channel routing — Muskingum: S = K[x I + (1 − x) O]; O₂ = C₀I₂ + C₁I₁ + C₂O₁; C₀ = (−Kx + 0.5Δt)/(K − Kx + 0.5Δt), C₁ = (Kx + 0.5Δt)/(K − Kx + 0.5Δt), C₂ = (K − Kx − 0.5Δt)/(K − Kx + 0.5Δt); C₀ + C₁ + C₂ = 1.
Muskingum x: 0 (reservoir) to 0.5 (pure translation); natural channels 0.1–0.3; K ≈ travel time; stability needs 2Kx ≤ Δt ≤ 2K(1 − x).
Hydraulic routing: Saint-Venant equations; kinematic & diffusion wave approximations; Muskingum–Cunge.
In level-pool routing the outflow peak lies on the falling limb of the inflow hydrograph (I = O at that instant, storage is maximum).
Experiments: Rainfall–runoff on hydrology bench (lag time, hydrograph shape), infiltration with double-ring infiltrometer, scour around bridge piers in a flume, stream gauging with current meter.
Scour: Local scour depth at piers increases with flow velocity, pier width and is reduced by pier nose shape/collar; Lacey normal scour depth R = 0.473 (Q/f)^(1/3).
Data handling: Plot contour/surface (Surfer) of scour bed; compare observed vs predicted using RMSE and R².
Symon's gauge = non-recording; tipping-bucket gives intensity; Thiessen polygons = area weights.
Horton: f = fc + (f₀ − fc)e^(−kt); φ-index ≥ W-index.
Unit hydrograph = 1 cm effective rain in D hours; S-curve changes duration; Qe = 2.778A/D.
